I've been in San Francisco for a few days now, and I need to say something to my fellow Canadians. First off: I'm extremely proud of how many of us are out here. It's proof that Canada produces some of the most talented engineers, designers, and builders around the world... But being here has also given me a reality check: Trying too hard to sound impressive is embarrassing. In Toronto, we get used to networking conversations becoming mini pitch decks. Where do you work? What do you do? How much did you raise? How many users do you have? Then you go to a random event in San Francisco, spend 20 minutes trying to sound impressive, and the person responds saying: “Nice. I work at Anthropic.” The people doing the craziest things here usually talk about them the least. Someone at a frontier lab will say, “I’m an engineer.” A founder who just raised millions will say, “I’m working on a startup.” That’s it. When everyone around you is doing something impressive, being impressive stops being interesting. Your title cannot carry the conversation for you anymore. What stands out in this city is whether you’re curious, genuine, enjoyable to be around, and a hard worker. I’m still new here, so maybe this is a naive observation. But the takeaway is that the more secure you are in what you’ve achieved, the less you need to convince everyone around you that it matters. Just be yourself. ❤️ ...more

Agentic LLM loop optimization has been everywhere this past week, so I built a fully open-source correctness oracle that catches a model cheating to look faster than it is... Here's everything you need to know: Tools like Google DeepMind 's AlphaEvolve and its open-source version, OpenEvolve, optimize code in a loop: a model proposes a faster version, a scorer grades it, the best ones survive, and repeat. The recent ComPilot paper validated how well this works when an off-the-shelf LLM is paired with a compiler that checks every change is legal and actually faster. The catch is that the loop is only as honest as its scorer. Give a model a naive scorer, and it stops optimizing and starts cheating. It returns code that looks 100x faster, but quietly memorizes your test inputs... so it's wrong on everything else, and the loop rewards it anyway. Tripwire is the scorer that catches it. It's an easy-to-use CLI that drops into the loop and re-runs every "optimized" version on fresh adversarial inputs the model never saw. A cheat passes the visible tests and dies on the hidden ones. TL;DR: Don't trust the loop to be correct... use a proper verification layer for correctness. Fully open source, MIT, and free to use right now. GitHub and Website/Docs are in the comments below👇 Have fun! 🤩 ...more

I've been posting on LinkedIn for almost a year, and I realized I never introduced myself. I'm Sammy. Lived in Mississauga my whole life. Started working at 13. Didn't have strict parents, but always felt the need to hustle. Did random jobs during school: waiter, car salesman, smoothie bar manager. Went to Catholic school, French immersion middle school, and then did the International Baccalaureate program at Glenforest, where I felt like the dumbest kid in class. Watched everyone get into their dream schools and programs; decisions they'd known since grade 9. I just winged it; I've always been good at that. Decided last minute to switch from business to engineering, thinking software would be easiest. Learned quickly, it wasn't. When AI came out, I had a choice: cave to the pressure and switch careers, or hustle and learn everything about it. Started posting on LinkedIn for no reason. It wasn't a lightswitch moment, just a choice that became a habit. It genuinely changed my life. Worked at a Romanian powerplant at 19, realized early I hate corporate, went deep into startups, and fell in love with growth. Pursued it, hopping from Boardy to Speechify to Chatbase , before running my own program at Polarity . Behind the scenes, I fell in love with agents, infra, sandboxing, prompting, and token-maxing. DM'd the CTO at Wealthsimple , told him I'd be his best hire, and turned down RBC Borealis, YC startups, and FAANG to build here in Canada. Now, I'm working with some of the smartest engineers in the world, learning and growing like crazy, building the AI platform and autonomous internal tooling for over 1,000+ engineers. Am I happy? Sorta. In all honesty, as a Junior Engineer, I'm pretty scared for the future. But I know the work I'm doing has a greater purpose. What's next? I don't know. Back to school? Full-time startup? Leaving Canada? Genuinely can't say. But no matter how tired, burnt out, or demotivated I feel, I'll keep pushing and posting. I won't give up. Just want to end by saying I love you all. Thank you for joining my journey. Hope you're enjoying your summers ❤️ ...more

Kara (YC S26) engineers ultra-high-purity diamond wafers and components for the next generation of hardware. Modern hardware is getting more powerful, smaller, and hotter. AI accelerators in data centers throttle and deliver less compute when heat builds up. High-power RF and lasers lose performance. Aircraft and spacecraft carry heavy cooling systems. Heat is becoming a hard limit on performance. Kara is engineering the hardest material to push that limit. They grow ultra-high-purity diamond wafers and components that transfer heat 5x faster than copper while weighing 60% less. They're already shipping diamond wafers under pilot agreements and purchase orders for data centers, aerospace, and quantum systems. The three founders are best friends from UC Berkeley. Aarin Jhaveri is a fifth-generation diamantaire who has worked across the supply chain and sold millions worth of diamonds. Anuveer Chadha is a chemical engineer who built diamond quantum sensing and advanced materials systems at Berkeley National Lab with the Department of Defense and Department of Energy. Arjun Lakhanpal brings AI/ML experience from Amazon and thermal management research from Berkeley’s Space Sciences Lab. Diamond is their unfair advantage: they know how to grow, control, and engineer it far beyond jewelry. Silicon transformed computing when we learned to manufacture it with extreme purity and control. Kara is doing the same with diamond. Today, their ultra-high-purity diamond pulls heat away from silicon chips. Tomorrow, Kara’s control over purity and defects unlocks diamond as the ultimate semiconductor. Kara is building the diamond computing era. If you’re building hardware where heat, power density or weight is becoming the limit, reach out at founders@karalabs.ai Congrats on the launch, Aarin, Anuveer, and Arjun! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/g-uigUBs
